# The phone run — Gemma 4 E2B on a Galaxy S26 Ultra, 2026-09-14

## Access and confidence

- **Device:** Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (SM-S938W), Android 16 (API 36),
  Snapdragon SM8750, 11.4 GB RAM — the exact model and chip Google's own
  Gemma 4 LiteRT-LM benchmark table names. Connected over USB, driven by
  `adb`; nothing on the phone was unlocked or accessed beyond what these
  two apps needed.
- **What ran:** the pocket-agent Kotlin example from this folder, built
  and installed fresh; the official Google AI Edge Gallery app (release
  1.0.19, the `sm8750`-matched build from its GitHub releases, since the
  Play Store was not used), with its own Benchmark screen, on Gemma 4 E2B.
- **What did not run:** the E4B, FunctionGemma, the Gallery's MCP or
  skills features, and Hermes on Termux — all still documented from
  their sources, not measured here.

## Trap: the GPU backend cannot write its cache to `/data/local/tmp`

The Kotlin example, unchanged from the laptop-build version, pointed at
`/data/local/tmp/gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm` (pushed there with `adb push`,
readable by the app). It failed to initialize on GPU with a bare "Failed
to create engine" on screen. `adb logcat` showed the real error:

```
E native  : E0000 … delegate_opencl.cc:340] Failed to create
litert::ml_drift::DelegateKernelLiteRt: INTERNAL: Could not open file
('/data/local/tmp/gemma-4-E2B-it.litertlm_1789324709_2588147712_mldrift_weight_cache.bin'):
Permission denied
```

The GPU backend writes a compiled weight-cache file *beside* the model
on first load — the same disk cache the CLI's `--cache disk` uses on the
laptop — and `/data/local/tmp` is shell's directory, not the app's; an
installed app can read what shell pushed there but cannot create a new
file in it. The fix: push the model to the app's own external-files
directory instead, which is writable without root —

```
adb shell mkdir -p /sdcard/Android/data/<package>/files
adb push model.litertlm /sdcard/Android/data/<package>/files/model.litertlm
```

— and point `modelPath` there. This is a general LiteRT-LM-on-Android
trap, not specific to this example: any app that lets the GPU backend
touch `/data/local/tmp` will hit the same permission error the first
time someone runs it on a real device rather than an emulator with a
looser SELinux policy.

## The Kotlin example, both backends

Same device, same model file (in the corrected location), one question
("Which outflows in 2026-08 are unclassified, and what did the cafe cost
in total?") through the two-tool preset:

| Backend | Engine start | Turn | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPU | 7,091 ms | 3,491 ms | Correct: 4 rows, $13.50 total |
| CPU | 3,434 ms | 7,407 ms | **Dropped one of the four rows** (NEWTOWN DENTAL) from the prose summary; the $13.50 total was still right |

CPU started faster than GPU — GPU's first load compiles an OpenCL kernel
graph, which the logcat showed replacing 100% of decode and prefill
nodes (`LITERT_CL`); CPU's XNNPack delegate covered only about 80% of
nodes but compiled faster. Once running, GPU's turn was roughly half
CPU's. The CPU's dropped row reproduces, on the phone, exactly what the
laptop run (`laptop-run.md`) found: a 2B model on CPU can execute a
two-tool call correctly and still misreport its own tool result in
prose. The number was never wrong; the summary was incomplete.

## The AI Edge Gallery's own benchmark

Menu → Models → Gemma-4-E2B-it → Benchmark. Defaults: 256 prefill / 256
decode tokens, 3 runs, averaged — the same 256/256 this guide's laptop
table already uses (not Google's own 1,024-token methodology).

| Backend | Prefill tok/s | Decode tok/s | Time to first token | First init | Steady init |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPU | 1,631.71 | 37.10 | 0.19 s | 12,671.95 ms | 6,057.62 ms |
| CPU | 273.76 | 26.36 | 1.00 s | 4,875.10 ms | 566.39 ms |

Against Google's published table for this exact device (E2B, S26 Ultra,
1,024/256 methodology): GPU claims 3,808 prefill / 52 decode; CPU claims
557 / 47. Measured here: GPU reached 43% of the claimed prefill rate and
71% of the claimed decode rate; CPU reached 49% and 56%. Time to first
token came in *faster* than claimed on both backends (0.19 s vs 0.3 s
claimed on GPU; 1.00 s vs 1.8 s on CPU) — not a contradiction so much as
a different prompt length: this benchmark's 256-token prefill has less
to read than Google's 1,024, so a lower absolute TTFT is expected even
at a lower throughput.

Against this laptop's own CLI benchmark (E2B, 256/256, M4 MacBook,
`laptop-run.md`): GPU 1,387 prefill / 76 decode; CPU 445 / 34. The
phone's GPU prefill (1,632) sits inside the laptop's own range; the
phone's CPU prefill (274) is well below the laptop's CPU prefill (445).
The flagship phone Google benchmarks did not outrun a two-year-old
consumer laptop on this measure — it matched it on GPU and trailed it on
CPU.

## What this changes about the guide's arithmetic

The guide's TL;DR and "what this means for choosing" sections used
Google's claimed GPU prefill rate to argue a Hermes-shaped turn
(~3,000 tokens) would read in "under a second" on this phone. At the
*measured* rate:

- 3,000 tokens ÷ 1,631.71 tok/s (GPU) = **1.84 s**
- 3,000 tokens ÷ 273.76 tok/s (CPU) = **10.96 s**
- 16,000 tokens ÷ 1,631.71 tok/s (GPU) = **9.81 s**
- 16,000 tokens ÷ 273.76 tok/s (CPU) = **58.45 s**

All four are corrected in the published guide; none of the original
"under a second" / "four seconds" / "half a minute" claims survived
contact with the actual device.
